newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka seen world's biggest tea exporter again.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka seen world's biggest tea exporter again.

text.p: Sri Lanka, overtaken by Kenya last year as the world's biggest exporter of tea, is likely to regain the top spot soon as privatisation of its plantations boosts harvests, industry experts said on Wednesday.

Most local industry forecasts predict Sri Lanka will produce more than 300 million kg a year of tea by 2002, up from around 250 million kg this year. Some estimates suggest output may even exceed 325 million kg a year by the same period.
Unless there is a similar radical increase in Kenyan tea production, which is generally considered unlikely, Sri Lanka should soon overhaul its rival, they say.
"I would say we will be the biggest tea exporter again very soon," said Anil Cooke, a director of Forbes & Walker Tea Brokers, which is part of plantation managing group Forbes Ceylon Ltd.
"We could definitely grow to 300 million kg output in five years' time," he added.

According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), Kenya exported 244.2 million kg of tea in 1996, just ahead of 244.0 million from Sri Lanka. Production was 257.2 million kg and 258.4 million respectively.
Tea is Sri Lanka's single biggest net foreign exchange earners, bringing in 34.1 billion rupees ($582 million) in 1996.
The government of Sri Lanka, formerly Ceylon, used to own and manage all the country's plantations, which produce tea, rubber and coconuts.
But amid signs of falling yields and heavy debts, it began restructuring the sector in 1992 by privatising the management of 23 plantation firms, which own some 600,000 hectares.

Privatisation of ownership began in 1995, when the government started selling 51 percent, or 10.2 million shares, of each company to a strategic investor, reserved 10 percent for workers and sold the balance of shares to the public.
Tea industry officials are confident the change in management and ownership will soon begin to reap rewards.

"The new firms are introducing better agricultural practices and better management," said Sudath Munasinghe, a director of tea operations at John Keells Holdings, which is now responsible for about one-fifth of Sri Lanka's tea output.
"Replanting is going ahead quickly. This is essential because some of our plants are very old," he said.
Munasinghe said the new tea companies had a strong incentive to boost production.
"All this time, managers were just managing. They had no proprietorial interest in the estates. But that is no longer the attitude," he said.
Soil reconditioning was proceeding with better fertilisers and manures after many years of poor husbandry, he added.

Yshan Fernando, director of the tea department at Eastern Brokers in Colombo, believes much of the new output will be from the poorer quality, low-grown tea sector, which accounts for about 55 percent of Sri Lanka's production.
But he said all grades of tea had scope for increases. "An increase to 300 million kg won't be difficult at all," he added.
Cooke agreed, saying Sri Lanka's acreage had been so badly under-utilised in the past that output could increase in future even if the new private firms used some land for other crops.
"Sri Lanka is way behind potential. Kenya, on the other hand, is reaching optimal production. It is stream-lined and well managed. Our plantations have not been," he said.
($1 = 58.6 rupees)
